title: Pablo Escobar Had So Much Cash, Rats Were Eating It
description: Pablo Escobar made so much money that his family wrote off ten percent of it every year to rats, water and rot. This is the story of how a tombstone thief from Medellin built one of the biggest criminal fortunes in history, why all that cash became his biggest problem, and how it all ended on a rooftop in 1993.

scenes.say: At the height of his power, Pablo Escobar had a problem most people will never have. He had so much cash that he couldn't spend it, couldn't bank it, and couldn't even protect it. Every year, his family simply wrote off ten percent of it. Rats ate it. Water rotted it. Some of it was buried and never found again.

huge stacks of hundred dollar bills in a dark room
a rat in a dark storage room
rotting wet dollar bills
a plastic barrel half buried in jungle soil

scenes.say: That isn't a legend from a TV show. It comes from his own brother, the man who kept the cartel's books. And it tells you something strange about money. When you have too much of it, and none of it is clean, it stops being an advantage and becomes a problem.

visuals.ai: an old handwritten accounting ledger with numbers

visuals.text: The rats would eat it in storage, or it would be damaged by water, or lost.
visuals.by: Roberto Escobar, Pablo's brother and the cartel's accountant

scenes.say: This is the story of how a small-time thief from Medellin became one of the richest criminals in history, how he spent his money, and how it all ended on a rooftop, the day after his forty fourth birthday.

visuals.sub: The money, the empire, the end

visuals.ai: the city of Medellin in a mountain valley at dusk
red tiled rooftops in a Colombian city

scenes.say: Pablo Emilio Escobar Gaviria was born on December first, 1949, in Rionegro, a small town in the green mountains of Colombia. His father was a farmer. His mother was a schoolteacher. The family was not rich, and young Pablo decided early that he would be.

visuals.ai: green Andes mountains with small farms in Colombia
a poor farm house in the Colombian mountains, 1950s

scenes.say: As a teenager in Medellin, he started small. He sold fake diplomas. He smuggled stereo equipment. And according to many accounts, he stole tombstones from cemeteries, sanded off the names, and sold them again.

visuals.ai: an old street in Medellin in the 1960s
an old fake diploma on a desk
old gravestones in a Latin American cemetery

scenes.say: By the early 1970s he had moved on to stealing cars. In 1974 he was arrested for car theft. It was a small crime. But Colombia was about to become the center of a much bigger business.

visuals.ai: a 1970s car on a Colombian street
a black and white police mugshot of a young man

scenes.say: In the 1970s, cocaine went from a rare drug to a booming market in the United States. The leaves were grown in Peru and Bolivia. The product was processed in Colombian jungle labs. And the customers were thousands of kilometres north.

visuals.ai: green coca leaves drying in the sun
thick jungle seen from above with a small clearing

scenes.say: Escobar understood something the old smugglers didn't. The real money wasn't in growing it. It was in controlling the route. In the mid seventies, he and a group of partners built what the world would later call the Medellin Cartel.

visuals.ai: a small propeller plane on a dirt airstrip
the Miami skyline in the 1980s at sunset

scenes.say: Small planes flew from hidden airstrips to islands in the Bahamas, and from there into Florida. By the mid eighties, American officials were saying the cartel controlled as much as eighty percent of the cocaine coming into the United States. Historians still argue about that number. But nobody argues about the money.

visuals.ai: a small tropical island with a runway, aerial view

visuals.label: Of the cocaine entering the US, according to US officials in the 1980s
visuals.note: An official estimate, still debated by historians

visuals.ai: a US Coast Guard boat on the sea, 1980s
piles of cash on a table

scenes.say: In 1987, Forbes magazine did something it had never done before. It put a drug trafficker on its list of the world's billionaires. Escobar's fortune was estimated at around two billion dollars. Two years later, the estimate was three billion.

visuals.title: Escobar's estimated fortune (US dollars)
visuals.note: Forbes estimates, as reported at the time

visuals.ai: 1980s New York business district

scenes.say: You may have seen bigger numbers online. Thirty billion. Even fifty billion. Those figures are not from Forbes. They were added years later. The real number was never audited, because the money never touched a real bank.

visuals.label: A number that spread online years later

scenes.say: Escobar spent like a man who knew it might all end tomorrow. He built a huge ranch called Hacienda Napoles. Over the entrance gate, he mounted a small airplane. And inside, he built his own private zoo.

visuals.ai: a ranch entrance gate with a small airplane mounted on top
a large tropical ranch with green hills
giraffes and zebras in a tropical ranch

scenes.say: Giraffes. Zebras. Elephants. And four hippos, flown in from abroad. Remember the hippos. They come back at the end of this story.

visuals.ai: a hippopotamus in a muddy tropical lake

visuals.label: Flown in for his private zoo in the 1980s

scenes.say: But here is the strange part. Most of that money was paper. Hundred dollar bills, fifty dollar bills, twenty dollar bills, flown back from America in bricks.

visuals.ai: close up of old hundred dollar bills
bricks of cash wrapped in plastic

scenes.say: According to his brother Roberto, the cartel spent about two thousand five hundred dollars a month just on rubber bands, to hold the stacks of bills together. Counting the money by hand took too long, so they simply weighed it.

visuals.ai: a pile of rubber bands on a table

visuals.label: Spent on rubber bands, according to Roberto Escobar

visuals.ai: an old money counting machine with cash
an industrial weighing scale with cash on it

scenes.say: The cash was hidden everywhere. In walls, under floors, in farmhouses, in barrels buried in fields. And because it couldn't go into a bank, a part of it slowly disappeared. About ten percent a year, his brother said, lost to rats, to damp, or to places nobody could remember.

visuals.ai: an old farmhouse in the Colombian countryside
cash hidden inside a broken wall
a blue barrel buried in a field
a rat chewing paper

visuals.label: Of the stored cash lost, according to Roberto Escobar
visuals.note: Rats, damp, and money that was never found again

scenes.say: Think about what that means. Ten percent a year is a loss most companies would never survive. For Escobar, it was just the cost of doing business. That is how much money was coming in.

visuals.ai: an enormous pile of cash in a warehouse

scenes.say: Money wasn't enough. Escobar wanted respect. He built football fields and paid for housing in the poor neighborhoods of Medellin, and many people there saw him as a hero. In 1982, he was even elected as an alternate member of Colombia's Congress.

visuals.ai: colorful small houses on a hillside in Medellin
a dusty neighborhood soccer field in Colombia
the Colombian national capitol building in Bogota

scenes.say: It didn't last. Colombia's justice minister, Rodrigo Lara Bonilla, exposed where Escobar's money came from, and Escobar was forced out of politics. In 1984, the minister was assassinated. It was the beginning of a war between Escobar and the Colombian state.

visuals.ai: a 1980s Colombian politician at a podium

scenes.say: His greatest fear was extradition. Being sent to an American prison, where his money and his men could not reach him. His group used a slogan: better a grave in Colombia than a prison cell in the United States.

visuals.ai: an American federal prison with high walls

visuals.text: Better a grave in Colombia than a prison cell in the United States.

visuals.ai: a tense Bogota street in the late 1980s

scenes.say: Cartel leaders even offered to pay off Colombia's foreign debt, around ten billion dollars at the time, in exchange for protection from extradition. The government refused. And the violence got worse. In November 1989, a bomb planted on an Avianca passenger jet killed more than one hundred people.

visuals.label: Colombia's foreign debt they offered to pay
visuals.note: Reported at the time; the offer came with demands

visuals.ai: a 1980s passenger jet on a runway

scenes.say: Then, in 1991, Colombia changed its constitution and banned extradition. That same day, Escobar surrendered. But he didn't go to a normal prison. He went to La Catedral, a prison he was allowed to build himself, on a hill overlooking Medellin.

visuals.ai: a prison complex on a green mountain above a city

scenes.say: The guards were reportedly chosen with his approval. Inside, there were comfortable rooms, a football pitch and a view of the city. He kept running his business from behind its walls.

visuals.ai: the ruins of a mountain prison with a city view
Medellin at night seen from a mountain

scenes.say: In July 1992, when the government tried to move him to a real prison, Escobar walked out. He escaped. And this time, everyone was hunting him.

visuals.ai: Colombian police officers in the early 1990s

scenes.say: A special police unit called the Search Bloc tracked him, with help from the United States. His rivals formed a group called Los Pepes to destroy his network. One by one, his men, his money and his hiding places disappeared.

visuals.ai: 1990s radio tracking equipment in a van
a police helicopter over a city
a quiet Medellin street with houses

scenes.say: He was running out of the one thing his money could never buy. Time. Some stories say that while hiding in the mountains, he burned around two million dollars in cash just to keep his daughter warm. That story comes from his son, and nobody can prove it.

visuals.ai: a small fire burning at night in the mountains

visuals.label: Burned to keep his daughter warm, according to his son

scenes.say: On December second, 1993, one day after his forty fourth birthday, police traced a phone call to a house in Medellin. Escobar ran across the rooftops. He was shot and killed. His family has always said he took his own life. Investigators concluded he was killed by police fire.

visuals.ai: an old 1990s telephone in a dark room
red tiled rooftops in Medellin
a grave in a green Colombian cemetery

scenes.say: So what does Pablo Escobar's fortune teach us about money? First, money you can't use isn't wealth. It's storage, and storage rots. Second, the more you have to hide, the more it costs you. And third, every fortune built on fear has an expiry date.

visuals.sub: about money, from Pablo Escobar's fortune

scenes.say: And the hippos? Escobar brought four of them to Colombia. After his death, nobody took them away. They escaped into the rivers and kept breeding. Scientists now estimate there are well over one hundred and fifty of them, and in 2026, Colombia approved a plan to cull up to eighty.

visuals.ai: hippos in a brown tropical river

visuals.title: Escobar's hippos
visuals.note: Estimates from Colombian scientists; 2022 study: about 170

visuals.ai: a hippo opening its huge mouth

scenes.say: Thirty years after his death, the most visible thing Pablo Escobar left behind is not his money. Most of it rotted, burned or was never found. It's a herd of hippos in a Colombian river.
